subChunks.title: Research Ethics & Scientific Integrity
subChunks.hookHtml:
'The Nuremberg Code was written in 1947,' Theodora said, 'by American judges in response to the trial of Nazi physicians who had conducted experiments on concentration camp prisoners without consent. It established ten principles for ethical human experimentation: voluntary consent is absolutely essential; the experiment must be necessary; risks must not outweigh benefits; the subject must be free to withdraw at any time. It was the first international standard for research ethics.'

'Then, in 1972, journalist Jean Heller broke the story of the Tuskegee syphilis study. Since 1932, the US Public Health Service had enrolled 399 Black men with syphilis in a study of the natural progression of the disease — and when penicillin became the established treatment in 1947, they were never told, never treated. The study continued until 1972. Six hundred participants. Four decades. The response: the National Research Act (1974), the Belmont Report (1979), and a permanent scar on trust between the US healthcare system and Black Americans that persists today.'

She looked up. 'Research ethics is not a bureaucratic compliance exercise. It is the accumulated response to actual catastrophes — things that happened to real people, often the most vulnerable, when scientists prioritised scientific knowledge over human dignity. Understanding why the rules are what they are is the foundation of practising them well.'
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Foundational Principles

The Belmont Report (1979) established three foundational principles for research involving human subjects: respect for persons (autonomy — individuals should be treated as agents capable of making their own decisions; those with diminished autonomy require special protection); beneficence (maximise benefits, minimise harms — including the injunction to first do no harm); and justice (fair distribution of research burdens and benefits — historically, vulnerable populations bore research risks while affluent populations received research benefits).

These three principles map onto procedural requirements: informed consent (respect for persons), risk-benefit assessment by an independent review board (beneficence), and equitable selection of research subjects (justice).

Informed Consent

Informed consent requires that prospective participants: receive complete, accurate, and comprehensible information about the research; understand the information; freely choose whether to participate without coercion or undue inducement; and retain the right to withdraw at any time without penalty. Exceptions: research involving minimal risk (anonymous surveys), emergency research (where consent is impossible), and deception research (where disclosure would invalidate the study — must include debriefing).

Challenges to genuine informed consent: length and complexity of consent forms (participants often do not read them); power differentials between researchers and participants (particularly in healthcare settings); cultural contexts where individual consent is not the relevant decision-making model; and online research where consent processes are routinely bypassed.

Research Integrity: Fabrication, Falsification, Manipulation

The US Office of Research Integrity (ORI) and equivalent bodies investigate three primary forms of research misconduct: fabrication (inventing data or results), falsification (manipulating or selectively omitting data), and plagiarism (using others' ideas or words without attribution). Collectively: FFP.

Major cases illuminate patterns: Diederik Stapel (social psychology) fabricated data in dozens of papers; Jan Hendrik Schön (condensed matter physics) fabricated results in high-profile papers in Science and Nature; Hwang Woo-suk (stem cells) fabricated cloning results that generated international investment and scientific excitement. In each case, institutional incentives (publish or perish, grant success metrics, institutional prestige) created environments in which misconduct was motivated and insufficiently checked.

Distinct from FFP, Questionable Research Practices (QRPs) are widespread and rarely investigated formally: p-hacking (trying multiple analyses until p < 0.05), HARKing (hypothesising after results are known), selective reporting of positive outcomes, rounding p-values down (0.054 → p < 0.05), inadequate sample size justification, and failure to report null results. QRPs are not usually investigated as misconduct but contribute substantially to the reproducibility crisis.

Research Ethics Beyond Human Subjects

Animal research ethics operates under the 3Rs framework (Russell and Burch 1959): Replace (use non-animal alternatives where possible — cell culture, organoids, computer models); Reduce (minimise animal numbers while maintaining statistical validity); Refine (minimise suffering and improve animal welfare in necessary experiments). In the UK, the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 requires project and personal licences for any regulated procedure on protected animals; in the US, the Animal Welfare Act and IACUC review apply.

Data ethics encompasses: privacy and confidentiality (General Data Protection Regulation in the EU; HIPAA in the US for health data); data sharing obligations (FAIR principles vs. participant privacy); secondary use of biobank data (broad consent vs. specific consent); and the use of clinical data for commercial machine learning.

Dual use refers to research with potential for both beneficial application and weaponisation. The H5N1 gain-of-function controversy (2011–2012): two research groups published work showing that H5N1 influenza could be made transmissible between ferrets by airborne route. The US NSABB (biosafety advisory board) initially recommended withholding publication methods; it later reversed the decision. The controversy opened a global debate about the boundaries of dual-use research oversight. CRISPR, synthetic biology, and artificial intelligence all raise dual-use concerns.

Ethics of Emerging Technologies

He Jiankui's creation of CRISPR-edited babies (2018) violated: informed consent principles (parents were not fully informed of risks); the principle of minimal risk (the health risks were substantial and uncertain); and the principle of justice (the children were harmed for a benefit to others). His sentence (3 years imprisonment) and the international condemnation that followed produced renewed calls for governance of human germline editing. The post-He landscape: WHO Advisory Committee on Human Genome Editing (2021) recommends against further germline editing pending governance framework development; UK HFEA maintains a ban on clinical germline editing.

storyBeats.text: 'The Belmont principles are abstract but the cases that generated them are not. Tuskegee is not a historical curiosity — its shadow falls on every conversation about vaccine hesitancy in Black communities today. The scar is real and earned. Ethics is not abstract. It is the scar tissue of catastrophe.'

'P-hacking is rarely treated as misconduct. But consider: if I test twenty analyses and report the one that gives p = 0.04, my false positive rate is not 5% — it is something closer to 65%. The statistical result is technically correct; the inference it invites is systematically misleading. QRPs are legal, common, and they corrode the evidential base of science.'

'Dual use has no clean solution. The knowledge that pathogen X can be made transmissible by route Y is simultaneously necessary for pandemic preparedness (we need to know what a pandemic pathogen might look like) and a potential recipe for harm. You cannot unknow things. The governance response is institutional — who has access, what safeguards, who decides — not a solution to the epistemological problem.'

'The 3Rs are excellent in principle and often honoured in bureaucratic form rather than spirit. Reduction requires genuine power analysis before experiments. Replacement requires investment in alternative methods that may not yet be as robust. Refinement requires honest self-assessment of animal welfare. The compliance approach — tick the box — defeats the ethical goal of the framework.'

Theodora looked at the consent form on the table. 'Twenty-three pages. A participant in our study is asked to read and sign twenty-three pages of legal text before providing a blood sample. Do we really believe they will read it? Do we believe the form reflects genuine understanding? The form protects the institution. That is not the same as informed consent.'

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what the three Belmont principles are and why each is important, using a concrete historical example where one of them was violated.
learningObjectives: Explain the historical origins of research ethics frameworks and connect specific cases to the principles they generated
Distinguish fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism from questionable research practices, and explain why QRPs contribute to the reproducibility crisis despite not being formal misconduct
Apply the 3Rs framework to a proposed animal research protocol, identifying opportunities for replacement, reduction, and refinement
Evaluate the governance challenges posed by dual-use research, with reference to the gain-of-function and CRISPR germline editing controversies
commonMistakes: Treating research ethics as synonymous with ethics committee approval — committee review is necessary but not sufficient for ethical research; researchers bear independent ethical responsibility

Distinguishing QRPs from FFP in a way that trivialises QRPs — p-hacking and HARKing have demonstrably large effects on the false positive rate in the literature and contribute as much to the reproducibility crisis as outright fraud

Assuming dual-use research governance can eliminate the problem rather than manage it — the knowledge is produced regardless, and governance decisions affect who has access and under what oversight, not whether the knowledge exists
Treating informed consent as a document-signing exercise rather than an ongoing process — consent can be withdrawn at any time, and the consent process should be proportionate to the risks involved
assessmentCriteria: Accurately connects historical cases of research ethics violations to the specific principles that emerged from them
Demonstrates understanding of the distinction between QRPs and FFP and explains the mechanism by which QRPs inflate false positive rates
Applies the Belmont framework to a novel research scenario, identifying the specific ethical obligations arising from each principle
Evaluates a dual-use scenario with appropriate appreciation of the tension between open science and biosafety, proposing a proportionate governance response
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Ethics Review of a Research Protocol

A researcher proposes the following study: 'We will recruit 200 participants from a hospital outpatient clinic waiting room. We will offer a £20 voucher to participate. Participants will complete a survey about their mental health history and current medication use. The survey will take 30 minutes. Data will be stored in an anonymised database accessible to research staff. Results may be shared with pharmaceutical companies for drug development.'

  1. Apply the three Belmont principles to this protocol. Identify at least one concern under each principle.
  2. Is the £20 voucher an inducement or coercion? What factors would affect your assessment?
  3. The data will be 'anonymised' and accessible to pharmaceutical companies. What concerns arise under data ethics, and what safeguards would you recommend?
  4. The hospital outpatient population is likely to include people experiencing health crises. What additional protections are required?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Belmont principles:

Respect for persons: Recruiting in a waiting room creates a coercive context — patients are anxious, time-pressured, and in a power relationship with the hospital. The capacity for free, uncoerced decision-making is compromised. Consent forms should be offered with explicit time to consider, in a private space, without the researcher present. The right to decline must be emphasised without any suggestion of consequences for healthcare.

Beneficence: Mental health history is sensitive personal information. The risk of psychological harm from completing a mental health survey (distress triggered by recollection) should be assessed. Safeguards: provide details of support services, allow participants to skip questions. The benefit — pharmaceutical research — is not a direct benefit to participants; the risk-benefit calculus must be explicit.

Justice: Hospital outpatient populations disproportionately include low-income, medically vulnerable, and ethnically marginalised individuals. Recruiting from this population for pharmaceutical company benefit without specific benefit to this population raises justice concerns. If the drug developed will be unaffordable to the population from whom data was collected, this is an unjust distribution of research burdens and benefits.

2. Inducement vs. coercion: A £20 voucher to a hospital outpatient — possibly unemployed, on a low income, or facing medical expenses — may constitute undue inducement: an offer sufficiently attractive that it impairs the ability to make a free decision. Assessment factors: (i) Is £20 proportionate to the time and risk? (ii) Is the population financially vulnerable? (iii) Would a reasonable person in this context feel they cannot afford to refuse? If the answer to iii is 'possibly yes', the inducement should be reduced or the recruitment population should be broadened. A flat voucher for all participants, regardless of income, risks disproportionately pressuring the poorest participants.

3. Data ethics: 'Anonymised' in practice means pseudonymised for mental health + medication data — re-identification is feasible using health records. Access by pharmaceutical companies for 'drug development' is vague — this could include commercial profiling. Concerns: (i) Is this secondary use covered by participants' consent? (ii) Does GDPR apply? (Health data is a special category under Article 9.) (iii) What safeguards govern pharmaceutical company access? Recommendations: specific consent for commercial data sharing (not bundled into general consent); data use agreement specifying what pharmaceutical companies can and cannot do; time-limited access; data destruction protocol.

4. Vulnerable population protections: The hospital outpatient population may include people with severe mental illness, acute psychiatric crises, or cognitive impairment. Additional protections: (i) Exclusion criteria for people in acute psychiatric crisis; (ii) assessor training to identify distress during recruitment; (iii) immediate referral pathway to clinical support; (iv) enhanced opt-out process — participants can withdraw data post-collection without consequence; (v) Independent patient and public involvement (PPI) in study design.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: In 2011, two research groups independently achieved what many biosafety experts had long feared: they created mutant H5N1 influenza strains transmissible between ferrets via the airborne route. Both groups sought to publish in Science and Nature. The US National Science Advisory Board for Biosecurity (NSABB) initially recommended withholding the methods from publication. Write a 350-word ethical analysis: (a) Why did the researchers believe the work was justified? (b) What are the strongest arguments for withholding publication methods? (c) What are the strongest arguments against withholding? (d) What governance mechanism would you recommend, and on what ethical grounds?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) Justification for the research: The researchers argued that: (i) Understanding what mutations confer airborne transmissibility is essential for pandemic preparedness — surveillance systems need to know what to look for in circulating strains; (ii) H5N1 has already evolved some transmissibility naturally, and the research revealed that adaptation required surprisingly few mutations, which is an urgent public health warning; (iii) The research could inform vaccine and antiviral development before a pandemic strain emerges naturally; (iv) The research was conducted in BSL-3 and BSL-4 facilities with appropriate biosafety protocols. The core claim: the pandemic risk from not knowing outweighs the risk from knowing.

(b) Arguments for withholding methods: (i) The methods constitute a blueprint for creating a pandemic pathogen; even if the risk from established national laboratories is low, the spread of methods through publication increases the risk from state actors and non-state actors with intermediate capabilities; (ii) The expected value of the biosafety knowledge may be lower than the expected value of the risk — surveillance systems do not need to know the exact mutational pathway to monitor for concerning mutations; (iii) The precedent of withholding methods for public safety is established (nuclear weapon design) and applicable here; (iv) Once published, the methods cannot be unpublished — the governance decision is irreversible.

(c) Arguments against withholding: (i) Selective withholding from journals while sharing with national security-cleared researchers creates an inequitable, opaque system; (ii) The information is likely discoverable by adversarial actors through alternative routes — withholding primarily disadvantages the legitimate scientific community; (iii) Secretive science undermines the norm of open, reproducible, cumulative knowledge that makes science trustworthy; (iv) There is no neutral governance body authorised to make such decisions globally — the NSABB has US jurisdiction only.

(d) Governance recommendation: Establish an international dual-use research review mechanism (akin to a safety advisory board with rotating membership from multiple countries) with authority to require staged disclosure: (1) share full methods with national public health authorities and WHO immediately; (2) publish scientific findings without methods in journals; (3) full methods released to scientists with institutional biosafety oversight after a 12-month review period. This balances scientific openness with proportionate risk management, avoids unilateral US jurisdiction, and preserves the public health knowledge function while reducing weaponisation risk.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The 1979 US report establishing three foundational principles for research ethics involving human subjects: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice — the basis for modern IRB/ethics committee review.
Behaviours that fall short of FFP (fabrication, falsification, plagiarism) but compromise research integrity, including p-hacking, HARKing, selective reporting, and underpowered studies.

Russell and Burch's (1959) ethical framework for animal research: Replace (use alternatives), Reduce (minimise numbers), Refine (minimise suffering) — now the standard for institutional animal ethics review.
Research that modifies pathogens to increase transmissibility, virulence, or host range — potentially valuable for pandemic preparedness but raising dual-use biosafety concerns.

The 2018 creation of CRISPR-edited human embryos (subsequently born as live infants) by Chinese researcher He Jiankui, resulting in his imprisonment and accelerated international governance debate on germline editing.

The suite of practices, norms, and training requirements that promote scientific integrity, including authorship practices, data management, conflict of interest disclosure, and mentoring obligations.

questions.questionHtml: What are the three principles established by the Belmont Report?
options: Respect for persons, beneficence, and justice
Informed consent, risk minimisation, and equitable subject selection
questions.correctAnswer: Respect for persons, beneficence, and justice
questions.explanationHtml: The Belmont Report (1979) established three principles: (1) Respect for persons — individuals are autonomous agents; those with diminished autonomy need protection; (2) Beneficence — maximise benefits and minimise harms; (3) Justice — equitable distribution of research burdens and benefits. These map onto procedural requirements: informed consent, risk-benefit review, and equitable subject selection respectively. Non-maleficence (do no harm) is a medical ethics principle from Beauchamp and Childress, not the Belmont Report specifically.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher runs 15 different statistical analyses on a dataset and reports only the analysis that gives p = 0.032, presenting it as if it were the pre-planned primary analysis. This is an example of which QRP, and what is its effect on the false positive rate?
options: P-hacking — the effective false positive rate is substantially higher than the nominal 5%, because multiple comparisons increase the probability that at least one test crosses the threshold by chance
HARKing — the researcher is presenting post-hoc hypotheses as pre-planned; this does not affect the statistical false positive rate
Fabrication — the researcher has manufactured a statistically significant result that did not exist in the data
Selective reporting — this is a minor methodological imperfection that has minimal effect on scientific conclusions
questions.correctAnswer: P-hacking — the effective false positive rate is substantially higher than the nominal 5%, because multiple comparisons increase the probability that at least one test crosses the threshold by chance
questions.explanationHtml: Running 15 analyses and reporting the one with p < 0.05 as if it were pre-planned is p-hacking. By chance alone, at α = 0.05, the probability of at least one false positive across 15 independent tests is 1 − (0.95)¹⁵ ≈ 54%. The reported p-value is nominally correct but the inference it invites (a 5% chance of a false positive) is wrong by an order of magnitude. This is distinct from fabrication (data are real) and from simple selective reporting (which also involves p-hacking). HARKing is the related practice of presenting post-hoc hypotheses as pre-specified.

questions.questionHtml: The 3Rs framework requires that animal experiments be 'replaced' where possible. Which of the following best illustrates a genuine replacement, versus a reduction or refinement?
options: Using a liver-on-a-chip microfluidic device instead of mouse hepatocytes to test drug metabolism — replacement of a living animal with a non-animal model
Using improved anaesthetic protocols during a surgical procedure — refinement of welfare during a necessary experiment
Using statistical power analysis to determine the minimum valid sample size — reduction in the number of animals used
Using higher-throughput screening to test more compounds per animal — reduction in the number of animals per compound tested
questions.correctAnswer: Using a liver-on-a-chip microfluidic device instead of mouse hepatocytes to test drug metabolism — replacement of a living animal with a non-animal model
questions.explanationHtml: Replacement means using a non-animal method where it is scientifically valid to do so. A liver-on-a-chip (human liver cells in a microfluidic device mimicking hepatic blood flow) replaces the animal as a model entirely. The other options are reduction (minimising animal numbers through statistical design or more efficient use) and refinement (improving welfare during experiments that still involve animals). The 3Rs hierarchy prioritises replacement first, then reduction, then refinement — but all three represent distinct ethical obligations.
